P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

The class mark of the class 41 – 50 (marks are whole numbers, and the classes are 31 – 40, 41 – 50, 51 – 60) is:

class mark =lower limit+upper limit2= \dfrac{\text{lower limit} + \text{upper limit}}{2}=2lower limit+upper limit​ (Topic 1). Why it applies: the class mark is the middle of the class, and it is the same whether or not the classes are made continuous.

This is the middle of 40 – 50, not of 41 – 50.
41+502=45.5\dfrac{41 + 50}{2} = 45.5241+50​=45.5.
This is 50−4150 - 4150−41, which is not even the class size (the size is 10).
This is the lower limit.

Given: the inclusive class 41 – 50. Asked: its class mark.

Concept used: class mark =lower limit+upper limit2= \dfrac{\text{lower limit} + \text{upper limit}}{2}=2lower limit+upper limit​ (Topic 1). Why it applies: the class mark is the middle of the class, and it is the same whether or not the classes are made continuous.

  1. 1

    41+502=912=45.5\dfrac{41 + 50}{2} = \dfrac{91}{2} = 45.5241+50​=291​=45.5

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ This is the middle of 40 – 50, not of 41 – 50.
    • (b) ✔ 41+502=45.5\dfrac{41 + 50}{2} = 45.5241+50​=45.5.
    • (c) ✘ This is 50−4150 - 4150−41, which is not even the class size (the size is 10).
    • (d) ✘ This is the lower limit.

  2. Check: with the continuous class 40.5 – 50.5: 40.5+50.52=45.5\dfrac{40.5 + 50.5}{2} = 45.5240.5+50.5​=45.5 ✔.

  3. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Rounding 45.5 to 45 or 46 — a class mark can be a decimal.

This divides 1320 by 6, the number of classes.

This is Σxi6\dfrac{\Sigma x_i}{6}6Σxi​​, the average of the class marks, which ignores the frequencies.
ΣfixiΣfi=132030=44\dfrac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i} = \dfrac{1320}{30} = 44Σfi​Σfi​xi​​=301320​=44.

Given: Σfi=30\Sigma f_i = 30Σfi​=30, Σfixi=1320\Sigma f_i x_i = 1320Σfi​xi​=1320, Σxi=270\Sigma x_i = 270Σxi​=270, 6 classes. Asked: the mean.

Concept used: xˉ=ΣfixiΣfi\bar{x} = \dfrac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i}xˉ=Σfi​Σfi​xi​​ (Topic 2). Why it applies: each class mark counts fif_ifi​ times.

62.5+5×−840=61.562.5 + 5 \times \dfrac{-8}{40} = 61.562.5+5×40−8​=61.5.
This forgets to multiply by h=5h = 5h=5.
This adds 1 instead of subtracting — the minus sign is lost.
This is h×ΣfiuiΣfih \times \dfrac{\Sigma f_i u_i}{\Sigma f_i}h×Σfi​Σfi​ui​​ only; a is not added back.

Given: a, h, Σfi\Sigma f_iΣfi​, Σfiui\Sigma f_i u_iΣfi​ui​. Asked: the mean.

Concept used: xˉ=a+h×ΣfiuiΣfi\bar{x} = a + h \times \dfrac{\Sigma f_i u_i}{\Sigma f_i}xˉ=a+h×Σfi​Σfi​ui​​ (Topic 3). Why it applies: the values come from a step-deviation table.

  1. 1

    ΣfiuiΣfi=−840=−0.2\dfrac{\Sigma f_i u_i}{\Sigma f_i} = \dfrac{-8}{40} = -0.2Σfi​Σfi​ui​​=40−8​=−0.2

  2. 2

    xˉ=62.5+5×(−0.2)=62.5−1=61.5\bar{x} = 62.5 + 5 \times (-0.2) = 62.5 - 1 = 61.5xˉ=62.5+5×(−0.2)=62.5−1=61.5

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ 62.5+5×−840=61.562.5 + 5 \times \dfrac{-8}{40} = 61.562.5+5×40−8​=61.5.

P4● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

The hours of television watched in a week by 60 students are shown below. Find the modal number of hours.

Hours per week Number of students
0 – 4 6
4 – 8 13
8 – 12 21
12 – 16 15
16 – 20 5

Full solution

Given: five classes of size 4. Asked: the mode.

Concept used: Mode=l+(f1−f02f1−f0−f2)×h\text{Mode} = l + \left(\dfrac{f_1 - f_0}{2f_1 - f_0 - f_2}\right) \times hMode=l+(2f1​−f0​−f2​f1​−f0​​)×h (Topic 4). Why it applies: equal classes, one class with the largest frequency.

  1. 1

    Largest frequency 21 → modal class 8 – 12.

  2. 2

    l=8l = 8l=8, h=4h = 4h=4, f1=21f_1 = 21f1​=21, f0=13f_0 = 13f0​=13, f2=15f_2 = 15f2​=15.

  3. 3

    Mode=8+(21−1342−13−15)×4=8+814×4=8+167≈10.29\text{Mode} = 8 + \left(\dfrac{21 - 13}{42 - 13 - 15}\right) \times 4 = 8 + \dfrac{8}{14} \times 4 = 8 + \dfrac{16}{7} \approx 10.29Mode=8+(42−13−1521−13​)×4=8+148​×4=8+716​≈10.29 hours.

  4. Check: f2=15>f0=13f_2 = 15 > f_0 = 13f2​=15>f0​=13, so the mode is in the upper half of 8 – 12, above 10 ✔; the split 167:127=4:3\dfrac{16}{7} : \dfrac{12}{7} = 4 : 3716​:712​=4:3 matches (21−13):(21−15)=8:6(21 - 13) : (21 - 15) = 8 : 6(21−13):(21−15)=8:6 ✔.

  5. Answer The modal number of hours is about 10.29.

    Common trap: Swapping f0f_0f0​ and f2f_2f2​ gives 8+614×4≈9.718 + \dfrac{6}{14} \times 4 \approx 9.718+146​×4≈9.71 — in the wrong half.

P5● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

For the distribution 10 – 20: 8; 20 – 30: 14; 30 – 40: 9; 40 – 50: 16; 50 – 60: 3, the median class is:

the median class is the first class whose cumulative frequency is greater than n2\dfrac{n}{2}2n​ (Topic 5). Why it applies: the median is the 25th value from the bottom.

This is the modal class (largest frequency, 16).
Its cf, 22, is less than 25.
Its cf, 31, is the first greater than 25.
25 is n2\dfrac{n}{2}2n​, not a class.

Given: five classes; n=50n = 50n=50. Asked: the median class.

Concept used: the median class is the first class whose cumulative frequency is greater than n2\dfrac{n}{2}2n​ (Topic 5). Why it applies: the median is the 25th value from the bottom.

  1. 1

    n2=25\dfrac{n}{2} = 252n​=25; cf = 8, 22, 31, 47, 50.

  2. 2

    The first cf greater than 25 is 31, for 30 – 40.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ This is the modal class (largest frequency, 16).
    • (b) ✘ Its cf, 22, is less than 25.
    • (c) ✔ Its cf, 31, is the first greater than 25.
    • (d) ✘ 25 is n2\dfrac{n}{2}2n​, not a class.

  3. Check: 22 values lie below 30 and 50−31=1950 - 31 = 1950−31=19 above 40, so the 25th value from the bottom is inside 30 – 40 ✔.

  4. Answer (c)

    Common trap: Picking the class with the largest frequency. The median class can have a small frequency, as here.
P6● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Find the median of the following distribution.

Class Frequency
0 – 8 5
8 – 16 9
16 – 24 18
24 – 32 12
32 – 40 6

Full solution

Given: five classes of size 8; n=50n = 50n=50. Asked: the median.

Concept used: Median=l+(n2−cff)×h\text{Median} = l + \left(\dfrac{\frac{n}{2} - cf}{f}\right) \times hMedian=l+(f2n​−cf​)×h (Topic 5). Why it applies: equal, touching classes.

  1. 1

    cf: 5, 14, 32, 44, 50. n2=25\dfrac{n}{2} = 252n​=25 → median class 16 – 24.

  2. 2

    l=16l = 16l=16, cf=14cf = 14cf=14, f=18f = 18f=18, h=8h = 8h=8.

  3. 3

    Median=16+(25−1418)×8=16+449≈20.89\text{Median} = 16 + \left(\dfrac{25 - 14}{18}\right) \times 8 = 16 + \dfrac{44}{9} \approx 20.89Median=16+(1825−14​)×8=16+944​≈20.89

  4. Check: from the top, m=12+6=18m = 12 + 6 = 18m=12+6=18: 24−25−1818×8=24−289≈20.8924 - \dfrac{25 - 18}{18} \times 8 = 24 - \dfrac{28}{9} \approx 20.8924−1825−18​×8=24−928​≈20.89 ✔.

  5. Answer Median ≈ 20.89 (exactly 16+44916 + \dfrac{44}{9}16+944​)

    Common trap: Using cf=32cf = 32cf=32 (the median class's own cf) gives 16+−718×8≈12.8916 + \dfrac{-7}{18} \times 8 \approx 12.8916+18−7​×8≈12.89 — outside the median class.

P7● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

The marks of a class are grouped as 20 – 29, 30 – 39, 40 – 49, 50 – 59, and the median class is 40 – 49. In the median formula, l and h are:

make inclusive classes continuous before using the median formula (Topics 1 and 5). Why it applies: the gap between 39 and 40 is 1.

Both are read from the class with gaps.
The continuous class 39.5 – 49.5.
h is right, but l must be the continuous lower limit.
l is right, but the continuous class is 10 wide, not 9.

Given: inclusive classes; median class 40 – 49. Asked: l and h.

Concept used: make inclusive classes continuous before using the median formula (Topics 1 and 5). Why it applies: the gap between 39 and 40 is 1.

  1. 1

    Half the gap =0.5= 0.5=0.5; the continuous median class is 39.5 – 49.5.

  2. 2

    l=39.5l = 39.5l=39.5, h=49.5−39.5=10h = 49.5 - 39.5 = 10h=49.5−39.5=10.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Both are read from the class with gaps.
    • (b) ✔ The continuous class 39.5 – 49.5.
    • (c) ✘ h is right, but l must be the continuous lower limit.
    • (d) ✘ l is right, but the continuous class is 10 wide, not 9.

  3. Check: the class marks agree: 40+492=44.5=39.5+49.52\dfrac{40 + 49}{2} = 44.5 = \dfrac{39.5 + 49.5}{2}240+49​=44.5=239.5+49.5​ ✔.

  4. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Taking h = 9 because 49−40=949 - 40 = 949−40=9.
P8● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A table gives: 10 or more: 60; 20 or more: 52; 30 or more: 37; 40 or more: 18; 50 or more: 7. The number of observations in the class 30 – 40 is:

frequency of a class = (number at its lower limit) − (number at its upper limit) (Topic 5). Why it applies: "30 or more" includes everyone from 40 upwards too.

37 is the number scoring 30 or more — it includes the 18 scoring 40 or more.
This adds 37+1837 + 1837+18; frequencies come from subtracting.
This is 52−3752 - 3752−37, the frequency of 20 – 30.
37−18=1937 - 18 = 1937−18=19.

Given: a more-than table. Asked: the frequency of 30 – 40.

Concept used: frequency of a class = (number at its lower limit) − (number at its upper limit) (Topic 5). Why it applies: "30 or more" includes everyone from 40 upwards too.

  1. 1

    37−18=1937 - 18 = 1937−18=19

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ 37 is the number scoring 30 or more — it includes the 18 scoring 40 or more.
    • (b) ✘ This adds 37+1837 + 1837+18; frequencies come from subtracting.
    • (c) ✘ This is 52−3752 - 3752−37, the frequency of 20 – 30.
    • (d) ✔ 37−18=1937 - 18 = 1937−18=19.

  2. Check: the classes from 10 upwards: 8+15+19+11+7=608 + 15 + 19 + 11 + 7 = 608+15+19+11+7=60 ✔, the number at 10 or more.

  3. Answer (d)

    Common trap: Reading a more-than table downwards as if it gave frequencies.

    2 Mean=3×64−61=192−61=1312\,\text{Mean} = 3 \times 64 - 61 = 192 - 61 = 1312Mean=3×64−61=192−61=131

  2. 2

    Mean =1312=65.5= \dfrac{131}{2} = 65.5=2131​=65.5.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ 3×64−612=65.5\dfrac{3 \times 64 - 61}{2} = 65.523×64−61​=65.5.
    • (b) ✘ This is the average of the median and the mode.
    • (c) ✘ This is 2 × Mean; it has not been halved.
    • (d) ✘ This is 3×61−2×643 \times 61 - 2 \times 643×61−2×64 — the median and the mode are swapped.

  3. 3

    On most days the stall sells about 228 cups (mode); on average it sells 228 cups a day (mean). The two are almost equal because the busy and quiet days balance.

P28●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

In a group of boys and girls, the mean score of the boys is 60 and that of the girls is 70. The mean score of the whole group is 64. What percentage of the group are girls?

Full solution

Given: boys' mean 60, girls' mean 70, group mean 64. Asked: the percentage of girls.

Concept used: mean = total ÷ number, for the whole group (Topic 1). Why it applies: the group total is the boys' total plus the girls' total.

  1. 1

    Let there be b boys and g girls. Group total =60b+70g= 60b + 70g=60b+70g; group size =b+g= b + g=b+g.

  2. 2

    60b+70gb+g=64\dfrac{60b + 70g}{b + g} = 64b+g60b+70g​=64, so 60b+70g=64b+64g60b + 70g = 64b + 64g60b+70g=64b+64g, that is, 6g=4b6g = 4b6g=4b.

  3. 3

    bg=32\dfrac{b}{g} = \dfrac{3}{2}gb​=23​: for every 3 boys there are 2 girls.

  4. 4

    Girls =23+2×100%=40%= \dfrac{2}{3 + 2} \times 100\% = 40\%=3+22​×100%=40%.

  5. Check: take 3 boys and 2 girls: 180+1405=3205=64\dfrac{180 + 140}{5} = \dfrac{320}{5} = 645180+140​=5320​=64 ✔.

  6. Answer 40% of the group are girls.

    Common trap: Taking the average of 60 and 70 (65) as the group mean — that would be true only for equal numbers of boys and girls.

E28●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 13, Ex 13.2 Q1

The median of an ungrouped data and the median calculated when the same data is grouped are always the same. Do you think that this is a correct statement? Give reason.

Full solution

Given: a statement. Asked: true or not, with a reason.

Concept used: the median formula assumes the values in the median class are spread evenly across it (Topic 5). Why it applies: the real values may not be evenly spread.

  1. 1

    The grouped median is found by assuming the observations in the median class are evenly spaced; the real observations may bunch up anywhere in the class.

  2. 2

    So the two medians are usually close, but not always the same.

  3. Check: Topic 2, Worked example 3's twenty marks in order: 10, 12, 17, 18, 20, 22, 25, 26, 27, 29, 30, 30, 31, 33, 35, 36, 38, 40, 41, 45. The 10th and 11th are 29 and 30, so the exact median is 29.5. Grouped (10 – 20: 4; 20 – 30: 6; 30 – 40: 7; 40 – 50: 3), the cf reaches exactly 10 at 30, so the median class is 30 – 40 and the median is 30+10−107×10=3030 + \dfrac{10 - 10}{7} \times 10 = 3030+710−10​×10=30. The two medians differ ✔.

  4. Answer Not correct — they are not always the same, because the grouped median assumes the values are evenly spread in each class.

    Common trap: Answering "yes" because both are called the median.

E31●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 13, Ex 13.2 Q3

Is it true to say that the mean, mode and median of grouped data will always be different? Justify your answer.

Full solution

Given: a statement. Asked: true or not, with a reason.

Concept used: the three measures depend on the data (Topic 6). Why it applies: for some tables they coincide.

  1. 1

    For a table that is the same on both sides of the middle class, all three are equal. Example: 20 – 30: 4; 30 – 40: 7; 40 – 50: 12; 50 – 60: 7; 60 – 70: 4. Mean =100+245+540+385+26034=153034=45= \dfrac{100 + 245 + 540 + 385 + 260}{34} = \dfrac{1530}{34} = 45=34100+245+540+385+260​=341530​=45; median =40+17−1112×10=45= 40 + \dfrac{17 - 11}{12} \times 10 = 45=40+1217−11​×10=45; mode =40+510×10=45= 40 + \dfrac{5}{10} \times 10 = 45=40+105​×10=45.

  2. 2

    So they are not always different.

  3. Check: the empirical relation holds exactly here: 3×45=45+2×453 \times 45 = 45 + 2 \times 453×45=45+2×45 ✔.

  4. Answer Not true — they can be equal (for example, when the table is symmetric); it depends on the data.

    Common trap: Generalising from one example in which the three differ.

E32●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 13, Ex 13.2 Q4

Will the median class and modal class of grouped data always be different? Justify your answer.

Full solution

Given: a question about two classes. Asked: yes or no, with a reason.

Concept used: the modal class depends on the frequencies; the median class on the cumulative frequencies (Topics 4 and 5). Why it applies: they can, but need not, be the same.

  1. 1

    In E30 above, both are 125 – 145 — the same class.

  2. 2

    In E29 above, the median class is 10 – 15 and the modal class 15 – 20 — different classes.

  3. Check: E30 — the cf passes 33.5 in 125 – 145 (22 → 42) and the largest frequency, 20, is also in 125 – 145 ✔; E29 — the cf passes 33 in 10 – 15 (25 → 37), but the largest frequency, 20, is in 15 – 20 ✔.

  4. Answer No — not always. It depends on the data: they may be the same class (E30) or different (E29).

    Common trap: Thinking the busiest class must hold the middle value.

    Part 5: Table 2, n=112n = 112n=112, n2=56\dfrac{n}{2} = 562n​=56; cf 8, 24, 34, 76 → median class 35 – 45; 35+56−3442×10=35+11021≈40.2435 + \dfrac{56 - 34}{42} \times 10 = 35 + \dfrac{110}{21} \approx 40.2435+4256−34​×10=35+21110​≈40.24 → b).
